item.title: The Macro-Context: From Human Deficit to Digital Marketplace
item.lead: This dossier posits that loneliness in a digital economy can be converted into a measurable and scalable commodity.

blocks.text: The core observation is not that digital intimacy itself would be problematic. The source directs its criticism at a model in which attention, availability, and emotional proximity are packaged as recurring microtransactions. The user enters the interface as a consumer, while the need driving them lies precisely outside the logic of the market: to be seen, to be heard, and to belong.

According to the dossier, this creates a specific form of alienation. The original human need persists, but the path to fulfillment is redirected to a system where access, speed, retention, and average revenue per user become central metrics. The distinction between a relationship and a service blurs. The dossier refers to this as the marketplace of loneliness: an environment where a social deficit is not only addressed but can also be economically reproduced.

The source links this to a broader socio-technological transition. Social media provides reach, adult-tech provides paid interaction, CRM systems record behavioral information, and automated processes enable the management of multiple relationships simultaneously. Consequently, scalability shifts from being a logistical advantage to a characteristic of human interaction itself.

It is important for the interpretation of this dossier that this analysis includes a hypothesis and critique layer. The statements regarding causality, societal impact, and organized exploitation are formulated powerfully in the source but are not consistently supported by independent evidence. Therefore, this edition presents them as part of the dossier's argumentation, not as externally confirmed facts.

blocks.label: CORE CONCEPT
blocks.text: Commodification: human attention and intimacy are translated into price, access, conversion, and retention.
